metadata.title: Object-Oriented Programming Knowledge Graph
metadata.description: A detailed connected graph of OOP foundations, object models, type systems, design principles, patterns, runtimes, languages, testing, persistence, security, and architecture.
metadata.scope_note: Language support is described at a high level; details can differ by standard version, runtime, and implementation. Some listed languages are functional-first or composition-oriented and are included to contrast OOP with adjacent paradigms.

entities.name: Object-oriented programming
entities.description: A programming paradigm that organizes software around objects that combine state, behavior, and identity; commonly uses abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.

entities.name: Object
entities.description: A runtime or conceptual entity that bundles data with operations and may have identity, state, and behavior.

entities.name: Class
entities.description: A definition describing the data representation and operations of instances; in some languages classes are also runtime objects.

entities.name: Instance
entities.description: A concrete object created according to a class or prototype-based construction process.

entities.name: Object state
entities.description: The values associated with an object at a particular time, often stored in fields or properties.

entities.name: Object behavior
entities.description: The operations an object can perform, typically exposed as methods or message handlers.

entities.name: Object identity
entities.description: The property that distinguishes one object from another even when their contents are equal.

entities.name: Method
entities.description: A function associated with a class, object, or prototype; instance methods commonly operate on a receiver.

entities.name: Field
entities.description: A named storage location belonging to an object or class.

entities.name: Property
entities.description: A named attribute whose access may be mediated by getters, setters, descriptors, or computed logic.

entities.name: Constructor
entities.description: A special operation or initialization protocol that establishes an object's valid initial state.

entities.name: Destructor
entities.description: A language-supported cleanup operation invoked at a defined lifecycle point in languages such as C++; not universal in OOP.

entities.name: Initializer
entities.description: An operation or protocol used to initialize an instance, distinct from allocation in some languages.

entities.name: Receiver
entities.description: The object or value to which a method call is directed, often named this, self, or me.

entities.name: this / self reference
entities.description: A language-specific reference to the current receiver; names and semantics differ across languages.

entities.name: Message passing
entities.description: A model in which objects interact by sending messages or invoking operations on one another.

entities.name: Encapsulation
entities.description: Combining data and operations behind a defined boundary and controlling how internal state is accessed.

entities.name: Information hiding
entities.description: Concealing implementation decisions behind stable interfaces so implementations can change without breaking clients.

entities.name: Abstraction
entities.description: Representing essential behavior while omitting irrelevant implementation detail.

entities.name: Inheritance
entities.description: A mechanism by which a type or object derives behavior or structure from another type or object.

entities.name: Single inheritance
entities.description: A class has at most one direct superclass.

entities.name: Multiple inheritance
entities.description: A class can inherit directly from more than one superclass, with language-specific conflict and layout rules.

entities.name: Multilevel inheritance
entities.description: An inheritance chain in which a derived type inherits from another derived type.

entities.name: Hierarchical inheritance
entities.description: Multiple derived types inherit from one common base type.

entities.name: Hybrid inheritance
entities.description: A combination of inheritance structures, sometimes including multiple and virtual inheritance.

entities.name: Composition
entities.description: Building a larger object from constituent objects whose lifetimes or ownership are treated as part of the whole.

entities.name: Aggregation
entities.description: A whole-part association where component objects can conceptually exist independently of the aggregate.

entities.name: Association
entities.description: A relationship in which objects know about, refer to, or collaborate with one another.

entities.name: Dependency
entities.description: A relationship in which one component temporarily uses another to perform work.

entities.name: Delegation
entities.description: An object forwards a responsibility to another object rather than implementing it itself.

entities.name: Polymorphism
entities.description: The ability to use a common interface while different concrete types provide different behavior.

entities.name: Subtype polymorphism
entities.description: Calls through a base type or interface can dispatch to implementations supplied by runtime subtypes.

entities.name: Parametric polymorphism
entities.description: Code is parameterized by types, commonly through generics or templates.

entities.name: Ad hoc polymorphism
entities.description: Different implementations are selected for a shared operation, for example overloads or type-class instances.

entities.name: Overloading
entities.description: Multiple declarations share a name but differ in parameter types, arity, or other language-defined signature elements.

entities.name: Overriding
entities.description: A subtype supplies a replacement implementation for an inherited virtual or dynamically dispatched operation.

entities.name: Dynamic dispatch
entities.description: The implementation invoked is selected at runtime according to the receiver's actual type or dispatch rules.

entities.name: Static dispatch
entities.description: The implementation is selected at compile time using static type information or a monomorphized specialization.

entities.name: Virtual method
entities.description: A method whose implementation may be selected dynamically through a base-class reference in languages with virtual dispatch.

entities.name: Interface
entities.description: A contract describing operations or capabilities without necessarily prescribing object representation.

entities.name: Abstract class
entities.description: A class that cannot be instantiated directly, often because it declares abstract operations or is intended as a shared base.

entities.name: Abstract method
entities.description: A method declaration without a concrete implementation in that type, requiring or permitting subclasses to provide one.

entities.name: Concrete class
entities.description: A class that can be instantiated and provides implementations required by its contracts.

entities.name: Trait / mixin
entities.description: A reusable unit of behavior or interface that can be composed into classes or types; exact semantics vary by language.

entities.name: Mixin
entities.description: A reusable behavior unit combined with another type, often without conventional single-root class inheritance.

entities.name: Protocol
entities.description: A named behavioral contract, notably in Swift and Objective-C, that types can conform to.

entities.name: Generic type
entities.description: A type parameterized by one or more type variables, enabling reusable abstractions with static or runtime checking.

entities.name: Template
entities.description: A compile-time parameterized definition in C++ and related languages, supporting types, values, and compile-time computation.

entities.name: Type parameter
entities.description: A variable standing for a type in a generic class, method, interface, or function.

entities.name: Variance
entities.description: Rules governing whether parameterized types preserve or reverse subtype relationships, or are invariant.

entities.name: Covariance
entities.description: A variance relation in which subtype relationships are preserved for a type parameter.

entities.name: Contravariance
entities.description: A variance relation in which subtype relationships are reversed for a type parameter.

entities.name: Invariance
entities.description: A rule that does not permit subtype conversion between differently parameterized forms based on the parameter subtype relation.

entities.name: Structural typing
entities.description: Compatibility determined by the shape or members of a type rather than solely by its declared name or ancestry.

entities.name: Nominal typing
entities.description: Compatibility determined by explicit declarations, names, or declared subtype relationships.

entities.name: Duck typing
entities.description: A dynamic typing style where an object is usable when it supports the operations required by a context.

entities.name: Subtyping
entities.description: A relation in which values of one type can be used where another type is expected, subject to substitutability rules.

entities.name: Liskov substitution principle
entities.description: A subtype should be usable wherever its base type is expected without violating the base type's behavioral guarantees.

entities.name: Open-closed principle
entities.description: Software entities should be open to extension while closed to modifications that destabilize existing behavior.

entities.name: SOLID principles
entities.description: A group of five object-oriented design principles: single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, and dependency inversion.

entities.name: Single responsibility principle
entities.description: A module or class should have one cohesive reason to change.

entities.name: Interface segregation principle
entities.description: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use; prefer focused contracts.

entities.name: Dependency inversion principle
entities.description: High-level policy and low-level details should depend on abstractions rather than directly on each other.

entities.name: DRY principle
entities.description: Avoid duplicating knowledge or logic; abstraction and reuse should reduce inconsistent repetition.

entities.name: KISS principle
entities.description: Prefer the simplest design that adequately solves the problem.

entities.name: YAGNI
entities.description: Do not implement speculative functionality before it is needed.

entities.name: Law of Demeter
entities.description: Limit coupling by having a component communicate primarily with its immediate collaborators.

entities.name: Design by contract
entities.description: Specify preconditions, postconditions, and invariants for operations and types.

entities.name: Class invariant
entities.description: A condition that must remain true for an object in all externally observable valid states.

entities.name: Precondition
entities.description: A condition that must hold before an operation is validly invoked.

entities.name: Postcondition
entities.description: A condition guaranteed after an operation completes under its contract.

entities.name: Immutability
entities.description: A property whereby an object's observable state cannot change after construction.

entities.name: Mutable object
entities.description: An object whose state can change after creation.

entities.name: Value object
entities.description: An object defined primarily by its values rather than unique identity, commonly immutable.

entities.name: Entity object
entities.description: A domain object whose identity persists even as some attributes change.

entities.name: Aggregate
entities.description: A domain-driven design consistency boundary containing an aggregate root and related objects.

entities.name: Aggregate root
entities.description: The primary entity through which external code accesses and enforces invariants for an aggregate.

entities.name: Domain model
entities.description: An object-oriented representation of business concepts, rules, and relationships in a problem domain.

entities.name: Data transfer object
entities.description: A data carrier used to move information between processes or architectural layers, typically with little domain behavior.

entities.name: Anemic domain model
entities.description: A domain model whose objects primarily expose data while domain rules and behavior are implemented elsewhere.

entities.name: God object
entities.description: An object that accumulates too many responsibilities and becomes a highly coupled central dependency.

entities.name: Feature envy
entities.description: A method that relies more on another object's data than on the data and behavior of its own class.

entities.name: Fragile base class
entities.description: A base-class change unintentionally breaks subclasses because inheritance couples implementation details.

entities.name: Diamond problem
entities.description: Ambiguity or duplication arising when a type inherits the same ancestor through multiple paths.

entities.name: Composition over inheritance
entities.description: Prefer assembling behavior from collaborators when it yields more flexible and less coupled designs than deep inheritance.

entities.name: Prototype
entities.description: An object used as a template from which other objects inherit or delegate behavior, often at runtime.

entities.name: Prototype chain
entities.description: A lookup chain through linked prototype objects used by prototype-based languages such as JavaScript.

entities.name: Class-based object model
entities.description: An object model where classes or class-like declarations define instance structure and behavior.

entities.name: Prototype-based object model
entities.description: An object model where objects delegate property lookup or behavior to other objects rather than requiring classes.

entities.name: Metaclass
entities.description: A class whose instances are classes; used to customize class creation and class-level behavior in languages such as Python.

entities.name: Reflection
entities.description: The ability to inspect types, members, annotations, or runtime objects programmatically.

entities.name: Introspection
entities.description: Runtime inspection of an object's type, members, or capabilities.

entities.name: Metaprogramming
entities.description: Programs or language facilities that generate, transform, or inspect other program structures.

entities.name: Annotation / attribute
entities.description: Metadata attached to declarations, types, methods, or fields, such as Java annotations or C# attributes.

entities.name: Access control
entities.description: Visibility rules such as public, protected, private, internal, or package-private.

entities.name: Public member
entities.description: A member accessible from contexts allowed by the language's public visibility rules.

entities.name: Protected member
entities.description: A member whose accessibility is generally limited to a type hierarchy or related contexts.

entities.name: Private member
entities.description: A member restricted to a class, object, or lexical scope according to language-specific rules.

entities.name: Static member
entities.description: A member associated with a class or type rather than each instance, although exact semantics vary.

entities.name: Instance member
entities.description: A member associated with a particular object instance.

entities.name: Class method
entities.description: A method whose receiver or binding is the class/type rather than a particular instance in languages that support it.

entities.name: Static method
entities.description: A method callable without an instance receiver and not automatically bound to instance state.

entities.name: Getter and setter
entities.description: Methods or property accessors used to read or update state while enforcing validation or computed behavior.

entities.name: Operator overloading
entities.description: A language facility allowing operators to be defined for user-defined types.

entities.name: Copy semantics
entities.description: Rules for creating an object from another object, including shallow/deep copies and language-defined copy operations.

entities.name: Move semantics
entities.description: Transfer of resources or state from one object to another, notably C++ move constructors and move assignment.

entities.name: Ownership
entities.description: Rules determining which value or scope is responsible for managing a resource or object's lifetime.

entities.name: Garbage collection
entities.description: Automatic reclamation of unreachable heap objects, used by Java, C#, Go, Python, JavaScript and other runtimes.

entities.name: Reference counting
entities.description: A memory-management strategy that tracks references and can reclaim objects when counts reach zero, sometimes supplemented by cycle detection.

entities.name: RAII
entities.description: C++ idiom tying resource acquisition and release to object lifetime through constructors and destructors.

entities.name: Object lifetime
entities.description: The interval from an object's creation or initialization until destruction or reclamation.

entities.name: Heap allocation
entities.description: Dynamic storage allocation often used for objects whose lifetime exceeds a lexical scope.

entities.name: Stack allocation
entities.description: Storage allocation tied to a call frame or lexical scope, where supported by the language and object model.

entities.name: Object serialization
entities.description: Transforming object state into a transportable or storable representation.

entities.name: Object deserialization
entities.description: Reconstructing data or objects from a serialized representation, with security and invariant concerns.

entities.name: Dependency injection
entities.description: Providing an object with collaborators from outside rather than constructing concrete dependencies internally.

entities.name: Factory Method
entities.description: Defines an interface for object creation while allowing subclasses or implementations to choose the concrete product.

entities.name: Abstract Factory
entities.description: Creates families of related objects through a shared factory interface.

entities.name: Builder
entities.description: Separates complex object construction from the final representation and can support staged or validated construction.

entities.name: Singleton
entities.description: Restricts a class or service to one shared instance within a defined scope; often introduces global-state and testability trade-offs.

entities.name: Prototype pattern
entities.description: Creates new objects by copying or cloning existing prototype instances.

entities.name: Adapter
entities.description: Wraps one interface so it can be used through another expected interface.

entities.name: Bridge
entities.description: Separates an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently.

entities.name: Composite
entities.description: Represents part-whole hierarchies so individual objects and groups share an interface.

entities.name: Decorator
entities.description: Adds responsibilities to an object by wrapping it with an object that implements the same or compatible interface.

entities.name: Facade
entities.description: Provides a simpler interface over a complex subsystem.

entities.name: Flyweight
entities.description: Shares intrinsic state among many logical objects to reduce memory use.

entities.name: Proxy
entities.description: Controls access to another object through a stand-in with a compatible interface.

entities.name: Chain of Responsibility
entities.description: Passes a request through handlers until one handles it or the chain ends.

entities.name: Command
entities.description: Encapsulates a request as an object, enabling queuing, logging, undo, or parameterized invocation.

entities.name: Interpreter pattern
entities.description: Represents a grammar or expression language as objects that can interpret or evaluate expressions.

entities.name: Iterator
entities.description: Provides sequential access to a collection without exposing its underlying representation.

entities.name: Mediator
entities.description: Centralizes communication among collaborating objects to reduce direct coupling.

entities.name: Memento
entities.description: Captures and restores an object's state without exposing its internal representation.

entities.name: Observer
entities.description: Defines a one-to-many notification relationship so dependents react to subject state changes.

entities.name: State pattern
entities.description: Changes an object's behavior by delegating to an object representing its current state.

entities.name: Strategy
entities.description: Encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface.

entities.name: Template Method
entities.description: Defines an algorithm skeleton in a base type while allowing subclasses to customize selected steps.

entities.name: Visitor
entities.description: Separates operations from object structures by dispatching visitors across element types.

entities.name: Repository pattern
entities.description: Mediates between domain logic and data mapping or persistence using a collection-like abstraction.

entities.name: Unit of Work
entities.description: Tracks changes during a business transaction and coordinates their persistence.

entities.name: Model–View–Controller
entities.description: Separates domain/state, presentation, and input/control responsibilities.

entities.name: Model–View–ViewModel
entities.description: Separates UI presentation from view state and interaction logic through a view-model abstraction.

entities.name: Object-relational mapping
entities.description: Maps objects and their relationships to relational tables and rows.

entities.name: Object-relational impedance mismatch
entities.description: Differences between object graphs and relational data models that complicate persistence mapping.

entities.name: Unit testing
entities.description: Tests a small unit, commonly a class or method, in isolation or with controlled collaborators.

entities.name: Mock object
entities.description: A test double that verifies expected interactions with collaborators.

entities.name: Test double
entities.description: A substitute used in tests, including mocks, stubs, fakes, and spies.

entities.name: Coupling and cohesion
entities.description: Coupling measures dependency between components; cohesion measures how well a component's responsibilities fit together.

entities.name: Refactoring
entities.description: Restructuring code without intentionally changing its externally observable behavior.

entities.name: Unified Modeling Language
entities.description: A standardized notation with class, object, sequence, component, and other diagrams used to model software systems.

entities.name: UML class diagram
entities.description: A diagram of classes, attributes, operations, and relationships such as association, generalization, dependency, and composition.

entities.name: UML sequence diagram
entities.description: A diagram showing object lifelines and messages in time order for an interaction.

entities.name: UML object diagram
entities.description: A snapshot of instances and links at a point in time.

entities.name: SOLID mnemonic
entities.description: Mnemonic for SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP.

entities.name: Prototype pollution
entities.description: A JavaScript-specific class of vulnerability where attacker-controlled property changes alter shared prototypes and affect other objects.

entities.name: Unsafe deserialization
entities.description: Deserializing untrusted data into objects can trigger unexpected behavior, gadget chains, or invariant violations.

entities.name: Mass assignment
entities.description: Automatically binding untrusted fields to object properties can expose protected state or privilege-related attributes.

entities.name: Encapsulation and security
entities.description: Encapsulation can support boundaries but is not a substitute for authorization, validation, or memory safety.

entities.name: Reflection security
entities.description: Reflective capabilities may bypass assumptions about visibility or enable dangerous dynamic invocation if exposed carelessly.

entities.name: Object concurrency safety
entities.description: Object design must account for shared mutable state, synchronization, immutability, and thread-safe publication.

entities.name: Actor object
entities.description: An object-like actor owns private state and processes messages, typically avoiding shared-memory mutation.

entities.name: Active Object
entities.description: Separates method invocation from execution so calls are queued and run by an object's own thread or executor.

entities.name: Event sourcing
entities.description: Persists domain changes as an ordered sequence of events from which state can be reconstructed.

entities.name: CQRS
entities.description: Separates command operations that change state from query operations that read state.

entities.name: Domain-driven design
entities.description: An approach that shapes software around a domain model, ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, and aggregates.

entities.name: Java
entities.description: Class-based, nominally typed language with single class inheritance, interfaces, dynamic dispatch, generics, annotations, reflection, and garbage collection.

entities.name: C++
entities.description: Multi-paradigm language with classes, multiple inheritance, virtual dispatch, templates, RAII, deterministic destructors, operator overloading, and value semantics.

entities.name: C#
entities.description: Class-based .NET language with interfaces, properties, virtual methods, records, generics, attributes, reflection, and garbage collection.

entities.name: Python
entities.description: Dynamic language whose object model treats nearly all values as objects; supports classes, multiple inheritance, descriptors, metaclasses, and duck typing.

entities.name: JavaScript
entities.description: Prototype-based language with dynamic objects, prototype delegation, classes as syntax over prototypes, closures, and first-class functions.

entities.name: TypeScript
entities.description: JavaScript superset adding static type checking, structural typing, interfaces, classes, access modifiers, generics, and type erasure at runtime.

entities.name: Ruby
entities.description: Dynamic, class-based language with open classes, mixins through modules, duck typing, blocks, and message-oriented object semantics.

entities.name: PHP
entities.description: Language with classes, interfaces, traits, visibility, inheritance, magic methods, and a runtime object model commonly used for web applications.

entities.name: Kotlin
entities.description: JVM and multiplatform language with classes, interfaces, data classes, sealed hierarchies, delegation, extension functions, and null-safety.

entities.name: Scala
entities.description: JVM and multiplatform language combining object-oriented and functional styles with classes, traits, case classes, enums, and advanced types.

entities.name: Swift
entities.description: Language with classes, structures, enumerations, protocols, protocol extensions, value semantics for structs/enums, and reference semantics for classes.

entities.name: Objective-C
entities.description: C-derived object-oriented language using Smalltalk-inspired message sending, dynamic runtime features, categories, protocols, and reference-counting/ARC conventions.

entities.name: Smalltalk
entities.description: Historically influential pure object-oriented language centered on objects, message sending, classes, and a live image-based environment.

entities.name: Simula
entities.description: Early language that introduced influential class and object concepts, inheritance, and simulation-oriented programming.

entities.name: C++ object model
entities.description: C++ object model includes subobjects, virtual bases, vtables as common implementation practice, object lifetime, and value/reference distinctions.

entities.name: Objective-C runtime
entities.description: Dynamic runtime that supports message dispatch, class metadata, categories, and runtime inspection.

entities.name: Java Virtual Machine
entities.description: Virtual machine executing JVM bytecode and providing class loading, verification, garbage collection, and runtime services.

entities.name: Common Language Runtime
entities.description: The .NET execution environment for managed languages, providing metadata, JIT compilation, garbage collection, and runtime services.

entities.name: JavaScript prototype runtime
entities.description: Runtime property lookup and method dispatch through object prototypes, including the behavior underlying class syntax.

entities.name: Python data model
entities.description: Special methods such as __new__, __init__, __getattribute__, descriptors, and metaclasses define Python object behavior.

entities.name: Garbage-collected runtime
entities.description: Runtime memory management that reclaims objects based on reachability; does not itself guarantee prompt external-resource cleanup.

entities.name: Automatic Reference Counting
entities.description: Compiler/runtime mechanism used by Objective-C and Swift reference types to manage strong references, with cycle-management considerations.

entities.name: C++ smart pointers
entities.description: RAII wrappers such as unique_ptr, shared_ptr, and weak_ptr encode ownership and sharing for dynamically allocated objects.

entities.name: std::unique_ptr
entities.description: C++ exclusive-ownership smart pointer that destroys its managed object when the owner is destroyed.

entities.name: std::shared_ptr
entities.description: C++ shared-ownership smart pointer that destroys its managed object when the final strong owner is released.

entities.name: std::weak_ptr
entities.description: C++ non-owning observer of a shared_ptr-managed object, useful for avoiding ownership cycles.

entities.name: Java default methods
entities.description: Interface methods with implementations, enabling interface evolution and reusable behavior without ordinary class inheritance.

entities.name: Records and data classes
entities.description: Language constructs for data-oriented classes with generated equality, representation, destructuring, or copy support; details vary by language.

entities.name: Sealed classes and hierarchies
entities.description: Restrict which types can extend or implement a type, enabling controlled hierarchies and exhaustive pattern matching in some languages.

entities.name: Extension methods
entities.description: Syntax for calling helper functions as if they were members, without necessarily modifying the original type.

entities.name: Language-level delegation
entities.description: A language construct that forwards interface implementation or behavior to another object, as in Kotlin by-delegation.

entities.name: Descriptors
entities.description: Python protocol for customizing attribute access, used by properties, methods, and many ORM fields.

entities.name: Objective-C categories
entities.description: Objective-C mechanism for adding methods to an existing class without subclassing, with constraints around stored state.

entities.name: Modules as mixins
entities.description: Ruby modules can be included or prepended to classes to compose behavior and alter method lookup.

entities.name: Traits in Rust
entities.description: Rust traits define shared behavior and support static or dynamic dispatch, but Rust is not class-based OOP and uses ownership rather than class inheritance.

entities.name: Interfaces in Go
entities.description: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly by method sets; embedding promotes methods and composition is idiomatic, without class inheritance.

entities.name: Rust
entities.description: Systems language supporting data types and trait-based polymorphism, ownership, borrowing, and composition; it deliberately does not use class inheritance.

entities.name: Go
entities.description: Language with structs, methods, implicit interfaces, embedding, and composition; it has no traditional class inheritance.

entities.name: Haskell
entities.description: Functional language that supports type classes and algebraic data types rather than conventional class-based OOP.

entities.name: Erlang
entities.description: Concurrent functional language whose process/actor model and message passing offer object-like encapsulation without conventional classes.

entities.name: Elixir
entities.description: BEAM language using immutable data and actor-like processes; it does not use traditional class-based objects.

entities.name: Fortran
entities.description: Scientific language supporting derived types, type-bound procedures, and type extension in modern standards.

entities.name: Ada
entities.description: Strongly typed language with tagged types, primitive operations, dispatching, interfaces, and controlled types.

entities.name: Object Pascal / Delphi
entities.description: Pascal family with classes, interfaces, inheritance, virtual methods, properties, and runtime type information.

entities.name: Visual Basic .NET
entities.description: Managed .NET language with classes, interfaces, inheritance, properties, and the CLR object model.

entities.name: Dart
entities.description: Class-based language with single class inheritance, interfaces by implementation, mixins, extension methods, and garbage collection.

entities.name: Perl
entities.description: Dynamic language with object systems based on packages/blessing and newer class features, plus roles through ecosystem modules.

entities.name: Raku
entities.description: Language with a rich object system including classes, roles, multiple dispatch, attributes, and metamodel capabilities.

entities.name: Groovy
entities.description: JVM language with Java interoperability, dynamic and static typing modes, traits, properties, metaprogramming, and closures.

entities.name: Clojure
entities.description: Functional Lisp on the JVM with immutable data and protocols/records/types for polymorphism, rather than conventional class-centric design.

entities.name: OCaml
entities.description: ML-family language with structural object types, classes, methods, inheritance, and a strong functional programming tradition.

entities.name: F#
entities.description: Functional-first .NET language with records, discriminated unions, interfaces, object expressions, and interoperability with .NET classes.

entities.name: Eiffel
entities.description: Class-based language emphasizing design by contract, inheritance, genericity, and assertions.

entities.name: Objective-C++
entities.description: Interoperability mode combining Objective-C objects/runtime with C++ types and deterministic resource management.

entities.name: Gang of Four design patterns
entities.description: Catalog of 23 classic object-oriented design patterns grouped into creational, structural, and behavioral families.

entities.name: Creational patterns
entities.description: Patterns that abstract or coordinate object creation, including Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, and Singleton.

entities.name: Structural patterns
entities.description: Patterns for composing classes and objects, including Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, and Proxy.

entities.name: Behavioral patterns
entities.description: Patterns for communication and responsibility, including Chain of Responsibility, Command, Iterator, Mediator, Observer, State, Strategy, Template Method, Visitor, and others.

entities.name: Object graph
entities.description: A network of objects connected by references, associations, containment, and other links.

entities.name: Aliasing
entities.description: Two or more references can reach the same mutable object, creating potential coupling and mutation visibility.

entities.name: Deep copy
entities.description: A copy that recursively duplicates reachable mutable components according to defined copying rules.

entities.name: Shallow copy
entities.description: A copy that duplicates the outer object while retaining references to nested objects.

entities.name: Object equality
entities.description: Rules for comparing objects by identity, value, or domain-specific equivalence.

entities.name: Equality/hash contract
entities.description: If objects compare equal under a hash-based collection's equality rules, their hash codes must satisfy the collection's contract.

entities.name: Exception handling
entities.description: Mechanisms for representing and propagating failures; constructors and object methods should preserve invariants when exceptions occur.

entities.name: Resource leak
entities.description: Failure to release external resources such as files, sockets, locks, or handles even if memory is garbage-collected.

entities.name: Dependency graph
entities.description: A directed graph of modules, classes, and services whose edges represent compile-time or runtime dependencies.

entities.name: Public API contract
entities.description: The stable externally visible types, operations, behavior, and compatibility promises offered by a component.

entities.name: Binary compatibility
entities.description: Whether compiled clients continue to link and execute after a library implementation or version changes.

entities.name: Serialization proxy pattern
entities.description: A serialization technique that reconstructs objects through a controlled proxy representation to preserve invariants and reduce attack surface.

entities.name: Visitor dispatch trade-off
entities.description: Visitor can make operations easy to add but often makes adding new element types harder, especially with closed type hierarchies.

entities.name: Inheritance and delegation taxonomy
entities.description: Relationships and mechanisms for code reuse and subtype behavior, with differing coupling and dispatch consequences.

relationships.description: OOP structures systems around objects and their collaborations.
A class commonly describes how instances are created and behave.
Objects may carry mutable or immutable state.
Behavior is offered through operations or message handling.
Identity distinguishes an object independently of its current field values.
Methods are a common way to express object behavior.
Fields commonly store object state.
Properties provide named access to stored or computed state.
An instance method normally operates on its receiver.
Languages use different keywords or implicit receiver conventions.
Construction establishes the initial state of an instance.
Initialization establishes values and invariants after or during allocation.
In languages with deterministic destruction, destructor execution participates in ending an object's lifetime.
Objects can collaborate through calls or messages.
Encapsulation is one of the central techniques associated with OOP.
Abstraction exposes essential contracts while hiding detail.
Inheritance is a reuse and subtype mechanism, but is not required for OOP.
Polymorphism lets clients work through common contracts.
Encapsulation can enforce boundaries that support information hiding.
Visibility restrictions limit direct access to implementation details.
Public is one possible member visibility level.
Protected is one possible member visibility level.
Private is one possible member visibility level.
Accessors can validate updates or compute values while preserving invariants.
A class typically declares or inherits methods.
A class may define per-instance fields or static fields.
A class provides a language-specific construction protocol.
Class members may have visibility modifiers.
Class-level members are shared or associated with a type rather than each instance.
Instance members belong to particular instances.
Some class declarations are intentionally non-instantiable.
Abstract classes can define required operations without implementations.
Concrete subclasses provide required implementations when the language requires it.
A class may implement an interface contract.
Traits or mixins can supply reusable methods and contracts.
A mixin contributes behavior to a host type.
Classes and value types can conform to protocols.
Class inheritance establishes subtype and reuse relationships.
Single inheritance limits each class to one direct superclass.
Multiple inheritance permits multiple direct superclasses.
Multilevel inheritance creates a chain of derived types.
Hierarchical inheritance has multiple children sharing a parent.
Hybrid inheritance combines inheritance structures.
Multiple inheritance paths can create ancestor ambiguity or duplication.
Subclasses may become coupled to undocumented base implementation details.
Composition is often preferable when reuse does not require a true subtype relationship.
Composition constructs an object from collaborators or components.
Aggregation is a whole-part form of association with independent component lifetimes.
Associations connect objects in an object graph.
A dependency indicates one component uses another.
An object can delegate responsibilities to a collaborator.
Objects commonly form a graph through references.
Associations and references define links between objects.
Multiple aliases can observe and mutate the same state.
Immutable state is safer to share because aliases cannot alter it.
Mutable objects permit state transitions.
Value objects are commonly compared by their meaningful values.
Entity objects retain identity even as their attributes change.
An aggregate is accessed through its root to enforce consistency.
The aggregate root coordinates changes to preserve aggregate invariants.
Domain models often include entities with identity.
Domain models often use value objects for descriptive concepts.
Aggregates define transactional consistency boundaries.
Domain-driven design develops a model that expresses domain concepts and rules.
DTOs primarily carry data and should not automatically be confused with rich domain objects.
An anemic model separates domain rules from data-bearing objects, often weakening encapsulation.
A god object tends to have low cohesion and high coupling.
Feature envy often signals misplaced responsibility or excessive coupling.
SRP is the first principle in SOLID.
OCP is one of the SOLID principles.
LSP is one of the SOLID principles.
ISP is one of the SOLID principles.
DIP is one of the SOLID principles.
SOLID is a mnemonic for five related object-oriented design principles.
A cohesive responsibility can improve cohesion and reduce unrelated change.
Stable abstractions and polymorphic extension can reduce changes to existing client code.
LSP describes behavioral requirements for substitutability.
Subtyping enables clients to use values through a common supertype.
ISP encourages narrow interfaces aligned to client needs.
Dependency injection is one practical way to depend on abstractions.
Interfaces can decouple high-level policy from implementation details.
Refactoring may remove duplicated knowledge while preserving behavior.
Simple object models are often easier to understand and maintain.
YAGNI cautions against speculative class hierarchies and unused extension points.
The Law of Demeter discourages long chains through unrelated object internals.
Contracts define conditions required before an operation.
Contracts define guarantees after an operation.
Contracts include conditions maintained across public operations.
A successful constructor should establish the class invariant.
Partially completed operations must avoid exposing invalid object state.
Subtype polymorphism dispatches behavior through a shared supertype.
Parametric polymorphism enables reusable algorithms over type parameters.
Ad hoc polymorphism selects behavior among distinct implementations.
Overridden virtual methods are commonly selected by runtime dispatch.
Overload resolution is commonly performed at compile time.
Virtual methods permit a call through a base interface to select a derived implementation.
C++ uses static dispatch for non-virtual calls and many template specializations.
Generic types declare type parameters.
C++ templates support compile-time parametric polymorphism.
Generic declarations may specify variance for their type parameters.
Covariance preserves subtype direction for a parameterized type.
Contravariance reverses subtype direction for a parameterized type.
Invariance disallows variance-based subtype conversion.
Structural subtyping uses member compatibility to establish substitutability.
Nominal subtyping follows explicit declared relationships.
Duck typing commonly relies on runtime behavior and supported operations rather than declared ancestry.
Operator overloads select operations based on operand types.
Records and data classes often make value-oriented modeling concise.
Sealed hierarchies constrain extension and can clarify a type's permitted variants.
Extension methods add convenient syntax without requiring changes to a type's declaration.
Language-level delegation can forward an interface implementation to a collaborator.
Python descriptors underpin property and other attribute access behavior.
A metaclass can control class construction in Python-like object systems.
Reflection often provides structured runtime introspection and invocation.
Metaprograms may inspect or transform program structures through reflection or compile-time facilities.
Metadata can be attached to classes and members.
Class methods commonly operate at the class level.
Static methods do not require a bound instance receiver.
Instance members include per-instance methods and fields.
Object state can be encoded for storage or communication, subject to format and compatibility rules.
Deserialization reconstructs data or objects from serialized representations.
Untrusted object reconstruction can invoke dangerous behavior or bypass invariants.
A serialization proxy can constrain reconstruction and preserve invariants.
Prototype chains implement inherited property lookup in prototype-based object models.
Prototype-based systems delegate lookup to prototype objects.
Class-based systems use class declarations or objects to define instance behavior.
JavaScript resolves inherited properties through prototype chains.
Prototype pollution alters shared prototype state and may affect unrelated objects.
Factories and injection can separate object creation from business logic.
Factory Method is a creational pattern.
Abstract Factory is a creational pattern.
Builder is a creational pattern.
Singleton is commonly catalogued as a creational pattern.
Prototype is a creational pattern distinct from prototype-based language semantics.
Adapter is a structural pattern.
Bridge is a structural pattern.
Composite is a structural pattern.
Decorator is a structural pattern.
Facade is a structural pattern.
Flyweight is a structural pattern.
Proxy is a structural pattern.
Chain of Responsibility is a behavioral pattern.
Command is a behavioral pattern.
Interpreter is a behavioral pattern.
Iterator is a behavioral pattern.
Mediator is a behavioral pattern.
Memento is a behavioral pattern.
Observer is a behavioral pattern.
State is a behavioral pattern.
Strategy is a behavioral pattern.
Template Method is a behavioral pattern.
Visitor is a behavioral pattern.
The classic design-pattern catalog groups creational patterns.
The classic design-pattern catalog groups structural patterns.
The classic design-pattern catalog groups behavioral patterns.
Builder separates staged object construction from the resulting product.
Factory methods encapsulate choices about which concrete object to instantiate.
Abstract factories create related objects through a family of interfaces.
Global singleton access can make dependencies implicit and testing harder.
An adapter presents an expected interface around an incompatible implementation.
Bridge lets abstraction and implementation vary independently.
Composite treats leaves and groups through a common interface.
Decorator adds behavior by wrapping a compatible object.
Facade hides a complex subsystem behind a smaller API.
Flyweight reduces memory by sharing common intrinsic data.
Proxy mediates access to a target object.
Observer notification communicates changes to dependent objects.
Strategy selects interchangeable algorithms through a shared contract.
State delegates behavior to a representation of the current state.
Command represents an action as an object.
Iterator separates traversal from collection internals.
Visitor commonly relies on dispatch across element types, with trade-offs when new element types are added.
Visitor favors adding operations over adding new element variants in classic implementations.
Repository gives domain logic a collection-like persistence abstraction.
Unit of Work tracks object changes during a transaction.
MVC separates model state and rules from view and controller responsibilities.
MVVM introduces a view-model between UI and domain or application state.
ORM maps object fields and relationships to relational persistence structures.
ORM tooling attempts to bridge object-graph and relational-model differences.
Unit tests often target class behavior and contracts.
A mock is a kind of test double focused on interaction expectations.
Test doubles isolate a unit from external collaborators.
Refactoring improves internal design without intentionally changing observable behavior.
UML includes class diagrams for static structure.
UML includes sequence diagrams for interactions over time.
UML includes object diagrams for instance snapshots.
Class diagrams represent classes, members, and type relationships.
Sequence diagrams can represent messages or method calls between lifelines.
Object diagrams depict concrete instances and links.
Immutable objects are easier to share safely across concurrent contexts.
Shared mutable objects may require synchronization or strict ownership rules.
Actors use asynchronous messages to interact while keeping state private.
Active objects often queue calls or messages for serialized execution.
Event-sourced entities reconstruct state from domain events.
CQRS separates write-side behavior from read-side projections.
Ownership models help determine when resources and objects are released.
RAII associates resource cleanup with deterministic object destruction.
Smart pointers express ownership or sharing through types and scope.
unique_ptr represents exclusive ownership.
shared_ptr represents reference-counted shared ownership.
weak_ptr observes a shared object without extending its strong ownership.
weak_ptr can break ownership cycles involving shared_ptr.
C++ idiomatic resource management often uses RAII and deterministic destructors.
The C++ standard library supplies ownership-aware smart pointers.
The managed object is destroyed when the unique owner releases it.
shared_ptr commonly uses a shared reference count to manage lifetime.
Garbage collectors reclaim unreachable managed objects, but external resources may need explicit cleanup.
Reference counts can trigger reclamation when no strong references remain.
ARC is compiler-assisted reference counting.
Java code commonly executes as bytecode on the JVM.
C# code commonly executes on the .NET CLR.
JavaScript's object model relies on prototype-based property lookup.
Python special methods and metaclasses define much of its object model.
The JVM reclaims unreachable managed objects through garbage collection.
The CLR garbage collector manages managed object memory.
Python implementations commonly combine reference counting with cyclic garbage collection.
JavaScript engines manage object memory through garbage collection.
Ruby implementations provide garbage-collected object memory.
Go uses garbage collection for managed heap objects.
Swift uses ARC for class instances; structures and enumerations have value semantics.
Objective-C object dispatch and metadata are supported by a dynamic runtime.
Objective-C applications can use ARC for automatic reference counting.
Python allows customization of class creation through metaclasses.
Python descriptors implement property access and method binding behavior.
Ruby modules can compose reusable behavior into classes.
Categories add methods to existing Objective-C classes.
Kotlin supports delegation of interface implementation to a supplied object.
Kotlin data classes generate common value-oriented methods.
Java records provide concise data-carrier classes with generated members.
C# records provide value-oriented equality and concise data modeling.
Scala case classes provide generated value-oriented behavior and pattern matching support.
Swift protocols define behavioral contracts for classes and value types.
Swift structs and enums commonly model value-oriented data.
Dart supports mixins as a behavior reuse mechanism.
Raku roles provide reusable behavior and interface composition.
OCaml includes classes and objects while retaining a strong functional style.
F# types can implement .NET interfaces and interoperate with class-based APIs.
Modern Fortran derived types and type-bound procedures support object-oriented designs.
Ada tagged types and dispatching operations provide object-oriented polymorphism.
Object Pascal and Delphi provide conventional classes, inheritance, and virtual methods.
Visual Basic .NET executes within the CLR.
Groovy integrates with the JVM and Java class ecosystem.
Scala commonly targets the JVM and interoperates with Java classes.
Kotlin commonly targets the JVM while also supporting other platforms.
Smalltalk emphasizes message sending as the central object interaction model.
Simula was historically influential in the development of class-based object concepts.
Rust uses traits and composition rather than conventional class inheritance.
Rust ownership and borrowing govern resource lifetimes and aliasing.
Go uses implicit interfaces and method sets for polymorphism.
Haskell type classes provide ad hoc polymorphism without conventional class inheritance.
Erlang processes encapsulate state and interact by message passing, although they are not class instances.
Elixir processes encapsulate state and communicate asynchronously rather than using conventional classes.
Perl supports object systems through packages, blessing, and evolving class syntax.
PHP traits provide a mechanism for horizontal code reuse.
Java supports interfaces, including default methods in modern versions.
Default methods let interfaces provide selected method implementations.
Java generics provide parameterized types with compile-time checking and type erasure at runtime.
C++ supports multiple inheritance with rules for ambiguity and virtual bases.
Python supports multiple inheritance and uses a method resolution order to determine lookup.
Ruby commonly uses modules and mixins instead of multiple class inheritance.
JavaScript is fundamentally prototype-based even though class syntax is available.
TypeScript's compatibility system is primarily structural.
Java class and interface subtyping is predominantly nominal.
C# class and interface subtyping is predominantly nominal.
Swift protocol conformance is central to abstraction and polymorphism.
C# has language-level properties with getters and setters.
Java reflection can inspect classes, fields, methods, and annotations at runtime.
The .NET reflection API inspects metadata and runtime types.
Python supports dynamic introspection of objects, classes, and modules.
JavaScript includes reflective facilities such as Reflect and property-descriptor APIs.
Objective-C message sends are resolved through runtime dispatch.
C++11 and later support move operations to transfer resources efficiently.
C++ defines copy constructors, copy assignment, and customizable copy behavior.
Python provides shallow and deep copy protocols through the copy module.
Languages differ in identity equality, value equality, and customization rules.
Hash-based containers require equality and hash code behavior to be consistent.
Shallow copies retain nested references, whereas deep copies recursively duplicate components according to defined rules.
Garbage collection of memory does not guarantee timely closure of files, sockets, or other external resources.
Depending on abstractions can reduce rigid links between high-level and low-level modules.
Changes to public types and members can affect source or binary compatibility.
Visibility contributes to design boundaries but does not replace security checks.
Reflection can expose powerful capabilities that must be controlled in security-sensitive contexts.
Unrestricted binding to object properties can let untrusted clients alter fields they should not control.
Prototype pollution is a known JavaScript object-model security issue.
Deserializing untrusted object graphs can lead to code execution or authorization errors in susceptible systems.
